assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 40,000 req/s peak. Desktop clients long-poll for changes, so 55% of all traffic is a notification poll that returns 'nothing changed'. Block download 25%, block upload 10%, metadata listing 9%, batch commit 1%.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Namespace cursors live in Redis, so a poll is answered without touching PostgreSQL 95% of the time (replica visit_prob 0.05). This is the single decision that keeps a 22,000 rps poll load off the database.

assumptions.subject: store
assumptions.statement: Content-addressed blocks of 'up to 4 megabytes', each named by 'a SHA-256 hash of the block' (Inside the Magic Pocket, dropbox.tech, 2016-05-06); 15% of downloads are served from the hot-block cache, the other 85% hit the object store. De-duplication means an upload does not always write a block - modelled optimistically as one write per upload. GAP: the same source says each block is 'stored independently in at least two separate zones', so a real upload is at least two block writes and this model UNDERSTATES the write load on this tier by roughly 2x. It is left at one write deliberately rather than doubled: doubling it would make the object store the binding constraint, and this tier's 20,000 rps capacity is an uncited guess (see the 'numbers' assumption), so there is no published figure that would justify pointing the reader there.

assumptions.subject: notify
assumptions.statement: Long-poll is modelled as a REQUEST, not a held connection: the engine is an open queueing network and cannot represent 10 million idle sockets. Sizing is therefore driven by poll RETURN rate, and the real constraint on this tier is file-descriptor/memory per connection, which this model does NOT capture. Dropbox re-architected exactly this tier: notification services 'can now be implemented via streaming gRPC instead of an expensive long-poll method' (How we migrated Dropbox from Nginx to Envoy, dropbox.tech, 2020-07-30), at 'tens of millions of open connections'. That is why this design leaves the notification tier as the highest-utilised component - in a file-sync backend it is the tier to look at first. Note that the front-door load balancer lands within a few points of this tier, so the engine reports the two as joint contenders rather than a winner: that is the honest reading, because they are the same connection-layer concern - every long-poll rides the LB before it reaches the notification service - and Dropbox's own edge post describes the pair together as 'tens of millions of open connections, millions of requests per second'.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: Compute only. Block-storage GB and egress are not priced here — at Dropbox's storage profile they dominate the real bill and list object-store rates would not be the rates paid.

assumptions.subject: block_api
assumptions.statement: Block data and metadata are SEPARATE tiers, so block transfer is not charged to the sync/metadata API. Dropbox documents 'two types of servers relevant to this discussion: Block data server ... Metadata server' and that 'the uploading client must talk directly with the blockserver in order to add these blocks' (Streaming File Synchronization, dropbox.tech, 2014-07-10). Drago et al. independently measured the same split in the wild as three client-facing subdomains - notification, meta-data control, and client storage - under the heading 'Clear separation between storage and meta-data/client control' (IMC 2012, authors' slide deck). An earlier version of this blueprint routed all 10,000 rps of block downloads through the metadata tier, which manufactured a metadata bottleneck the real architecture does not have and sent the reader to optimise the wrong component.

assumptions.subject: upload_block
assumptions.statement: An upload is TWO metadata round trips, not one: the client commits, the server replies 'need blocks', the client uploads the missing blocks to the blockserver, and the client commits again (Streaming File Synchronization, dropbox.tech, 2014-07-10). upload_block therefore visits the sync/metadata API with visit_prob 2.0 and the block tier with 1.0.

assumptions.subject: numbers
assumptions.statement: NO Dropbox source publishes a per-tier request rate or an absolute latency, so every per_instance_rps and base_latency_ms in this file is an uncited assumption and must not be read as a measurement. What Dropbox publishes is aggregate or relative only: 'at least 300,000 requests per second' across '700M registered users' (Atlas, 2021-03-04); Edgestore 'serving more than ten million requests per second' (2018-11-09); Cape at '30K/s' events and '150K/s' jobs (Cape technical deep dive, 2018-12-21); and for Magic Pocket only deltas, e.g. 'a 2% increase in Magic Pocket's overall end-to-end write latency' with no absolute figure anywhere in that post (2022-12-08). The new block tier is therefore sized by COPYING the metadata tier's per-instance capacity (1,500 rps) and service time (12 ms) rather than inventing a distinct figure for it; its 16 instances were chosen to carry its 14,000 rps well inside the 85% ceiling, not fitted to a published number.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The real metadata store is SHARDED MySQL, not one PostgreSQL primary: Edgestore is 'a service and abstraction over thousands of MySQL nodes', with a caching layer absorbing 'upwards of 95% of client reads' (Cross-shard transactions at 10 million requests per second, dropbox.tech, 2018-11-09). At this blueprint's 40,000 rps the single primary stays well inside its capacity, so the simplification does not move the bottleneck - but a reader must not carry the single-primary shape up to Dropbox's real scale, and it is also this model's only single point of failure.

assumptions.subject: flow_mix
assumptions.statement: The 10:1 block-to-commit ratio here (upload_block 0.10 vs commit_batch 0.01) implies an average committed file of about 40 MB in 4 MB blocks. Drago et al. measured roughly 80% of storage flows carrying 10 chunks or fewer (IMC 2012 slide deck), so real files are smaller and commit_batch is under-weighted relative to block traffic. Left unchanged because commit_batch's 400 rps is nowhere near binding on any tier; a reader modelling a small-file workload should raise it.

assumptions.subject: evidence_vintage
assumptions.statement: Dating the evidence: Drago et al. measured Dropbox desktop client v1.2.52 in 2012, and Dropbox shipped a full sync-engine rewrite (Nucleus) to all users on 2020-03-09 (Rewriting the heart of our sync engine, dropbox.tech). The 2012 measurements are cited here as evidence of the TIER SEPARATION - block vs metadata vs notification - and not as evidence about today's internals.

_library.summary: File-sync backend: long-poll change notification, a block data tier the client talks to directly (separate from metadata), a content-addressed block store, and a cursor cache that keeps polling off the metadata database.
